"Conceivably" means "in a way that is possible to imagine."

When you say something is conceivable, you mean your mind can picture it happening — it's not impossible. So when you say "conceivably," you're saying: "I can imagine this being true or possible, even if I'm not certain."

The root idea here is conceiving — not in the sense of having a baby, but in the older sense: forming an idea in your mind. To conceive of something means to be able to picture it mentally.

So "conceivably" = "in a way that the mind can picture as possible."

This is a word of cautious possibility. It sits in the space between "this will definitely happen" and "this is impossible." When someone uses it, they're essentially saying:

"I'm not promising this, but I can imagine it being true."

It's honest and careful. It doesn't overclaim. It signals that the speaker is opening a door of possibility, but not fully walking through it.

Here are several examples across different situations, with explanations:

Example 1:

"This could conceivably be the best film made in the last decade."

What it means: The speaker isn't declaring it the best film — they're saying "I can imagine making the case that it is." It's praise, but tempered with intellectual humility.

Example 2:

"If the train is delayed, we could conceivably miss the entire first half."

What it means: Missing the first half isn't certain, but it's a real possibility the speaker can picture. The word warns without panicking.

Example 3:

"He could conceivably win the election, but it would take a lot of things going his way."

What it means: A win isn't predicted — it's just within the range of imagination. Often this kind of sentence implies the possibility is surprising or unlikely, but not impossible.

Example 4:

"How could anyone conceivably believe that?"

What it means: This is a rhetorical use — the speaker is saying it's hard to even imagine believing something. Here "conceivably" is used to express disbelief or incredulity.
A Key Nuance: It Often Implies "Even If Unlikely"

This is subtle but important. Compare:

  • "It's possibly raining in Mumbai." → Neutral statement of possibility.
  • "It could conceivably snow in Mumbai." → The possibility exists, but it's unusual. The word conceivably here subtly signals: "Yes, I can imagine it, but I'm aware it's a stretch."

So "conceivably" often carries a slight implication that the possibility is at the outer edge of what seems realistic. It acknowledges something could happen while hinting that it might require a bit of imagination to believe.

This makes it more vivid than "possibly." It says: "I had to actually picture this in my mind to arrive at it."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Possibly:
More neutral. Just says something might happen. No suggestion that it requires imagination.

"It will possibly rain today." (straightforward, weather-based probability)

Conceivably:
More imaginative. Suggests the speaker actively pictured it and found it within the range of possibility, perhaps against their initial instinct.

"It could conceivably snow in Chennai in December." (possible, but requires effort to picture)

Theoretically:
Based on logic or rules, not necessarily on imagination. If the rules don't prevent something, it's "theoretically" possible.

"Theoretically, you could drive from Delhi to London." (the logic works, the physics allow it — but practically, no.)

Conceivably is warmer and more human than theoretically. It's about the imagination, not just logic.

Imaginably:
Very similar to conceivably, but rarer. "Conceivably" is the more natural, common choice in modern English.

You'll almost always see "conceivably" in sentences that also use modal verbs like could, might, may, can:

  • "This could conceivably work."
  • "She might conceivably agree to it."
  • "He can conceivably finish by Friday."

It rarely stands alone or starts a sentence. It lives inside a sentence, usually right after a modal verb or the word "not":

  • "I cannot conceivably understand why he did that." (= I can't even imagine understanding it)

"Conceivably" is a slightly formal or careful word. You'll hear it in:

  • Journalism and analysis ("This policy could conceivably affect millions.")
  • Academic or professional writing
  • Careful, thoughtful speech

In casual conversation, people might just say "maybe" or "possibly." But when someone says "conceivably," they usually want to sound more precise — they're being deliberate about the kind of possibility they mean.

The word is essentially your mind's way of keeping doors open. When you say something is conceivable, you're not predicting it — you're simply refusing to rule it out. And conceivably, as the adverb, is the word you use to wear that careful, honest uncertainty on your sleeve.
